
##### samhan › Queen Sunduk (632)
[0] p: A Queen? Ridiculous.
[1] p: Munhee (26) is a young noblewoman, being attended by her low-rank servants. She is getting her hair done for an important event, while a servant takes care of her baby son Inmun (3).
[2] D(munhee): Totally unfit for a Noble woman… Come on, boy, can’t you find something better?
[3] p: Her husband Chunchu is dressing too. He is twenty-nine, and already the most cunning man in Samhan. Only the quiet rooms know it yet. Their two children are getting under everyone's feet.
[4] hanja: {"kind":"hanja","chars":[{"char":"春","gloss":"봄 춘","meaning":"spring"},{"char":"秋","gloss":"가을 추","meaning":"autumn"}],"name":"Chunchu","ko":"춘추","note":"Spring and autumn. Also the name of the oldest
[5] p: Bupmin is six. He finds his father and uncle on the hill where adults invent countries and sits down without being asked.
[6] D(munmu): When I’m king everyone has to listen to me. / Even the bone people. / …And the ones with no bone. Those most, there’s more of them.
[7] D(munhee): Listen to him. / He gets the sentences from you. The volume is his own.
[8] D(chunchu): …Keep that. / I may need to borrow it back when I am braver.
[9] p: Before they dress for the hall he takes the two of them around the palace road. Gotaso sits in front of him on the same horse. Bupmin has his own, and will not share the saddle.
[10] D(gotaso): Faster. / Father. Faster.
[11] D(chunchu): You'll bite your tongue. / Then you'll talk less, which — wait, that's the joke? Fine. Hold on.
[12] D(munmu): I'm not racing. / I'm following. That's different.
[13] D(chunchu): That's a lawyer's horse, son. / Look at you. I'm going to tell your mother you invented a new kind of slow.
[14] p: King Jinpyung (65) is dead, after years of expanding Silla against Baekje.
[15] p: Silla runs on bone. Your rank is your birth, and your birth is your life. Six common ranks at the bottom. Above them, the nobles. Above them, the royals.
[16] diagram: Bone Rank · 골품제
[17] p: In the hall the sleeves are the census. True Bone wears purple 자색. Head Rank Six wears scarlet 비색. Five wears blue 청색. Four and below wear yellow 황색. You can read a man before he speaks.
[18] D(alchun): Below all of them are the slaves — but those are not counted as people.
[19] D(sunduk): …A country that does not count people as people. How is that meant to last a thousand years?
[20] p: Three royals are left. All three are the old king's daughters. Dukman, thirty-seven. Seungman, thirty-two. Chunmyung, fifty-two. That is the whole bloodline, and all of it is women.
[21] p: Which of the three it will be is settled the night before, in a pavilion off the pond, by six men and a brazier. By morning the palace has a name, and the name has to be dressed.
[22] D(sunduk): I put on this confident face, / but honestly — me, becoming king… / I wonder whether I can do it at all…
[23] D(yushin): Whether you do it well or badly — / that is what “no matter what” means. / In all this world, wouldn’t it be good to have one person always on your side, Princess? / Hwarang Kim Yushin. / I will serve you to the end.
[24] p: And so she becomes the first Queen of Silla. They will call her Queen Sunduk, the Blue Moon of the Divine Country.
[25] QUOTE: 聖骨男盡 故女王立 || The sacred-bone males were exhausted, and therefore a queen was set up. || Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Royal Chronology (王曆) — Queen Seondeok
[26] table: {"kind":"table","head":["Queen","Crown Princess","Crown Prince","High Councillor","Marshal"],"rows":[["Sunduk (37) 선덕여왕","Kim Seungman (32)","Kim Chunchu (29)","Euljé (60) 을제","Yushin (37) 유신"]]}
[27] p: Munhee's big brother is Yushin. He is thirty-seven, and he runs the yard. Horse, bow, gyuku: that is where boys learn whether they matter. People call him the Sword of Silla. He is also, everyone notices, very fond of the princess.
[28] p: The capital’s daughters follow the Sword of Silla around the yard. He does not look at them. He looks only at the Queen.
[29] D(courtmaid): The marshal walked past. / I know. Don’t look. / …I’m looking.
[30] D(courtmaid): The most popular man in Silla, and he will not even turn his head. / If he smiled once the colonnade would fall over.
[31] p: Then the yard-coat is open down the spine, and She sees the width of his back — muscle the court is not supposed to want — and the Queen’s face goes vermilion before she can pretend it is the lamp.
[32] p: He and Chunchu had known each other since they were boys. There is a story about that, though neither of them tells it the same way twice.
[33] flashback: the east star
[34] D(yushin): Are you feeling alright, your majesty?
[35] D(sunduk): Hm? (startled)
[36] D(yushin): Look at me. / Not the door. (smiles)
[37] p: For a moment neither of them says anything. Then she straightens, and she is the Queen again.
[38] D(yushin): …Once.
[39] D(sunduk): Once what.
[40] D(yushin): Call me by name, not by title. / Today, since it is the last day for it.
[41] D(sunduk): …Yushin-ah.
[42] p: Nobody in the room hears it. It is the last time in forty-one years that anyone calls him that, and he will still be able to hear it on the day he dies.
[43] D(sunduk): Lord Yushin. / My sister married for love and got a son out of it. / I got a council that sat until dawn.
[44] D(yushin): …Your Majesty.
[45] D(sunduk): So from now on — «Your Majesty». Nothing else. / …That is what I have.
[46] p: Then the young knights kneel and pledge themselves to the throne. Bidam kneels in front, already the yard's Second Blade. Pumsuk is fourteen, and trying very hard not to look it.
[47] D(hwarang): By Hyukgosé’s light, we, the young Hwarang knights of Silla, pledge eternal allegiance to the Queen!
[48] p: At the end of the ceremony, everyone chants for their new queen.
[49] p: May the heavenly White Horse bless this queen… Long live the Queen! Long live the Hwarang spirit! Long live Silla!
[50] D(undefined): (market woman, to a child) / Remember where you live. The Divine Country. The Rooster Forest. / Kings change. Get the name right.
[51] p: Blue banners. A moon no one has to point at. In the capital they have already raised a tower to read the stars — Cheomseongdae.
[52] p: Silla sends envoys to the other kingdoms to let them know of their new queen.
[53] D(kingmu): So that old brat Jinpyung is finally dead… Bah! Good riddance. And they have seated a daughter, eh…?
[54] D(yeongnyu): Let us see how long that Council of theirs lasts.
[55] D(taizong): A woman king… those Samhan barbarians are at it again, aren’t they? Wu! Prepare my robes.
[56] p: He sends her a gift: a painting of peonies in three colours, and a packet of their seeds.
[57] D(sunduk): …There are no butterflies on these flowers.
[58] D(alchun): Your Majesty?
[59] D(sunduk): It means no scent. / …And the Second Emperor would like me to know he has noticed I have no husband.
[60] p: She has the seeds planted anyway. When they bloom, they have no scent. The court decides she is a sage. She knows she simply reads people.
[61] D(jomei): First my aunt, and now Silla as well…? It must be a new trend.
[62] p: Sun, for kindness.
[63] p: Duk, for virtue.
[64] hanja: {"kind":"hanja","chars":[{"char":"善","gloss":"착할 선","meaning":"goodness; kindness"},{"char":"德","gloss":"덕 덕","meaning":"virtue"}],"after":"Long live Queen Sunduk!","name":"Sunduk","ko":
[65] p: Six men who hate the word “woman” crowned one anyway. How? Go back one night, to a brazier…!

##### samhan › Harmony Council (632)
[0] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"The Night Before","ko":"전날 밤"}
[1] p: The Harmony Council meets to debate who the next king should be. Six nobles, one night. Nobody stands up until they all agree.
[2] p: Night in a small pavilion off the pond. Someone lights the small brazier. The flame is red first.
[3] p: It runs hotter. The flame turns blue. Only then may the session start.
[4] p: Each sleeve has a cup of tea and a wooden piece on a personal mat. They vote by setting the piece on either side of the cup.
[5] p: The Council decides by unanimity. One voice against is enough to stop a name. That is why it takes all night, and why the room fears the newest member almost as much as it fears a woman on the throne.
[6] p: The first count is three to three. A hung jury in silk. Initial vote, then deliberation, then a final vote that cannot move until every sleeve agrees.
[7] p: Three pieces go to the yes side of the cup. Three go to the no side.
[8] diagram: Initial vote · 초투표 3:3
[9] D(alchun): The first count is split. / Half this room still says a woman cannot rule.
[10] p: How about Prince Chunchu…? Chunchu’s mother is a Royal, but his father is a Noble… In that case, the child becomes a Noble as well.
[11] flashback: The night bridge · 귀교
[12] p: How about the Kim of Gaya…? The Marshal’s blood is royal — in a country that no longer exists. Yes, and if we begin counting kingdoms that no longer exist, half this room is royal.
[13] p: The Royal blood, there remain only three… The woman king, finally we shall see…
[14] p: The newest member of the Council — a Hwarang barely seated among them — stands up.
[15] D(bidam): My lords have said one word forty times tonight. “Woman.” / I have known Princess Dukman since I was a boy. / Not one of you has ever put a question to her that she could not answer. / If only three of the Sacred Bone remain, then I choose the cleverest of the three.
[16] D(murim): …If cleverness picks a king, whose cleverness do we hear tomorrow. / Bone is the measure. Bone does not change.
[17] D(imjong): The bone has run out. / Holding a country on empty bone is more dangerous than a clever woman.
[18] D(suljong): I still… cannot raise my hand. / This room is too old to be turned by one night’s speech.
[19] D(yushin): I have put questions to her. / They were answered. Half this room never asked — they only repeated the word woman. / That is what deliberation is for. To overturn the first count.
[20] D(yumjang): …Alchun. Only your hand is left.
[21] D(alchun): I have taken a tiger. / A tiger has no sex. It has teeth. / …I raise it. Final vote.
[22] p: Alchun moves his piece. All six sit on the yes side.
[23] diagram: Final vote · 최종 투표 6:0
[24] D(alchun): …That boy Bidam has no fear in him at all.
[25] p: Across the floor, Yushin catches the Second Blade's eye. He and Bidam have been trading wins since they were boys in the yard. The count stands at one hundred and eight apiece. Neither lets the other stay ahead for long.
[26] D(yushin): Well stood. / Tomorrow on the yard — the hundred-and-ninth is mine.
[27] D(bidam): Come now, brother. / Today is the country’s business. The blade can wait till tomorrow.
[28] cite: High Councillor
[29] p: They argue past midnight. In the end there is nothing left to argue with — the blood runs out before the objections do, and Dukman is queen.
[30] p: Every sleeve in that room learned to fight in one dead king’s yard. Who was he? Back we go, to the Cloud King…!

##### samhan › Jinheung, the Cloud (554)
[0] p: Ask anyone in Surabol about the Cloud King and they'll tell you about his stones. Ask anyone in Sabi and they'll change the subject. You'll find out why. Not yet.
[1] p: He was seven when they put the crown on him. It was too big, and nobody mentioned it. By the end, Silla had a river, a coastline and Gaya. He got there by being the best ally in Samhan, right up until the afternoon he wasn't.
[2] p: He put up stones wherever he stopped — four of them, on mountains, at the edges of what he had taken — and the stones do not boast. They say who came, and when, and that the land is now inside the border. They are property deeds.
[3] D(herald): There is no boasting on this stone at all.
[4] D(herald): Boasting is for men who are worried about losing it.
[5] p: Late in his reign he invents the Hwarang. Take the noblest boys and put them in one yard. Make them ride, sing and rank each other until the ranking feels like fate. Nearly every man who matters later comes out of that yard.
[6] p: One class a year. The number sticks to a man for life. Almost every sleeve on the Council first slept in that hall.
[7] diagram: The Hwarang · 화랑
[8] p: Chunchu. Yushin. Bidam. Pumsuk. Alchun. Gwanchang. Wonsul. They are all, in the end, one old man’s idea about what to do with teenage boys.
[9] p: Near the end he shaved his head. The king of the four mountain stones put on a monk's robe and took a new name: Dharma Cloud. His queen went into a nunnery beside him. The court kept calling him Majesty. He kept answering to the other thing.
[10] p: Long after the stones are mossed over, the old men of the capital still argue about what to call him. Not in the official registers — those keep to temple names — but in the quiet after the wine.
[11] D(undefined): Jinheung… we called him the Cloud King. After the name he took at the end. / A cloud has no border, you see. It goes where it likes, and for an afternoon the ground underneath is its ground.
[12] D(herald): That sounds like praise.
[13] D(undefined): It was, for about a year. / Then you look at where the shade fell. Gwansan. The Han. Gaya. / A cloud never asks whose field it’s raining on.
[14] p: That rain fell on Baekje’s field. Baekje kept the grudge. Now meet the prince who will inherit it…!

##### samhan › Prince Euija (632)
[0] p: Thirty-two is late to be named crown prince. By the time his father gets around to it, Euija has more than fifteen sons. The clans have had years to decide which ones they own.
[1] hanja: {"kind":"hanja","chars":[{"char":"義","gloss":"옳을 의","meaning":"righteous"},{"char":"慈","gloss":"사랑 자","meaning":"merciful"}],"name":"Euija","ko":"의자","note":"Righteous and merciful. His father chose i
[2] p: In Sabi the clans read the stars the way other courts read ledgers. Loyalty is the word they use when the door between king and house is still closed; after it opens, they use other words.
[3] D(herald): …Fifteen?
[4] D(herald): His Majesty has over fifty — Samsin must keep a night shift just for Sabi. The Crown Prince is still comfortably behind.
[5] p: This is said admiringly. It is that kind of court.
[6] p: The young princes grow up already spoken for. Yung is the eldest. Pung is eight and has good handwriting. Each boy wears a clan's ring, hears a clan's tutor, and finds a clan's grudge folded into his allowance.
[7] D(kingmu): Crown Prince. / There. Now they have to bow to you first and complain about you second.
[8] D(euija): They complained first for thirty-two years, Father. / I’ll take the bow.
[9] cite: Prince Euija (32)
[10] p: Euija sneaks out of the palace to explore the life of the common people.
[11] p: The boy is going back into the water. He has been at it since morning, and he is not a strong swimmer.
[12] D(euija): How many times have you gone in?
[13] D(gyebek): Nineteen.
[14] D(euija): …You were counting?
[15] D(gyebek): At twenty I would not come back out. That is why I count.
[16] D(euija): <b>Are you insane?! In that much of a hurry to stand before Yumla?!</b>
[17] D(gyebek): I gave my word.
[18] p: It takes a while to get it out of him.
[19] flashback: No name
[20] D(euija): A fine young man… what is your name?
[21] D(gyebek): I have… no name.
[22] D(euija): …What? You think it makes sense to have no name, here in Baekje?
[23] D(euija): It’s the name of a great man. / How about — “Gyebek”?
[24] p: It is the White River — the wide mouth below Sabi where clan barges quarrel over winter space, and where boys who cannot swim keep trying anyway.
[25] D(gyebek): …Do you like the name, or do you like me?
[26] D(euija): …People don’t usually ask that.
[27] D(gyebek): I have to ask, or I do not know.
[28] p: Prince Yung is the favored one to win — oldest, strongest, and backed the way favorites are always backed: by houses that have already counted what he will owe them. In the succession the clans are not watching. They are holding the brackets.
[29] p: Eight houses. Eight fighting styles. One king between them. And every house has already picked a prince…!

##### samhan › Eight Great Clans (632)
[0] p: Satek. Yunbi. Jinmo. Mokli. Hae. Baek. Guk. Ahn.
[1] p: The Eight Great Clans run this country, and one king sits between them. Satek fights with the king's sleeve. Yunbi fights with the coast road. The other six keep their techniques quiet.
[2] table: {"kind":"table","head":["Jinmo","Satek","Yunbi","Mokli","Hae","Baek","Guk","Ahn"],"rows":[["진모","사택","연비","목리","해","백","국","안"],["眞牟","沙宅","燕比","木刕","解","苩","國","安"]]}
[3] p: Once a year, the court chalks a square grid in the palace yard. Four hard lines. No banners. The young men of each house step onto the grid in white. It's the same quarrel as the west bridge, only without the carts.
[4] D(eldersatek): White cloth. Wooden swords. / If anyone bleeds the wrong colour, the berth talks stop for a month.
[5] D(elderyunbi): Then keep your boys’ wrists honest. / The chalk does not care whose sleeve they hold.
[6] p: Swords first. Wooden ones, which still remember steel. A Jinmo boy holds his blade high. A Satek boy answers from the middle. On the call they both move. Blades skim the chalk. The white sleeves clap together so close that the steps gasp.
[7] D(undefined): That Jinmo boy? / Short wrists. / Feet faster than the Satek though. / Point to the white sleeve.
[8] p: When the wooden points are tallied, the sand comes out. A circle of grit inside the same square. Ssireum — satba locked before they stand, knees in the grit, equal grips on waist and thigh, then up without letting go. No circling for a hold. The bout is the hold.
[9] p: A Hae boy hooks a leg. A Guk boy answers with his hip. He lifts, he turns, and the other boy's feet leave the earth. The yard goes quiet the way a dock goes quiet when a rope snaps. Sand takes the shoulder. The chalk does not argue.
[10] D(eldersatek): See? / Even Yunbi can fall without a cart.
[11] D(elderyunbi): Your boy’s knee touched first. / Ask the chalk. / Elders watch from the hall steps — they always do — and still count wrong when it is their sleeve.
[12] p: By dusk the white is grey with chalk and grit. Nobody has settled four generations of anything. The throne likes it that way. The boys go home with a score instead of a funeral.
[13] p: The Satek clan is currently the most powerful. Both the Queen and the Premier are from the Satek clan, making them a key rival to the royal Buyeo clan.
[14] cite: Elder Satek
[15] cite: Minister Satek
[16] cite: Queen Satek
[17] cite: Satek Chunbok
[18] p: In the Assembly they fight for power, each house holding a share of the king's sons. They fight in the street too. Same fight. The street version is older.
[19] diagram: Eight Great Clans · 대성팔족
[20] diagram: Ministers’ Assembly · 정사암회의
[21] p: Unlike Silla’s Harmony Council, the Assembly does not require every voice. A plurality of houses is enough — which is why the street fights matter. Votes can be bought in pieces. In Surabol they must be bought entire, or not at all.
[22] p: What the Assembly votes on, more often than war, is water. Who loads first. Whose ships winter in the river mouth. Who gets the orange levy, and who gets the silk berth. In this country, a clan without a harbour can't feed a fight.
[23] D(eldersatek): Yunbi talks of blood. / We talk of berths. / Blood cools. A winter anchorage does not.
[24] D(elderyunbi): You hold the king’s sleeve and call it a harbour. / We hold the coast road. Sabi to the salt. Every cart that fears rain pays us in quiet.
[25] p: Satek and Yunbi have been at it for four generations. Nobody alive can say what started it. Everybody alive can list the last six things.
[26] D(undefined): The Yunbi boys turned a Satek cart over at the west bridge yesterday. / Then tonight the Satek go over a Yunbi wall. / Same as the lantern festival last year. / Last year three of them died.
[27] D(eldersatek): Yunbi is not Baekje blood. They rolled in from the north.
[28] D(elderyunbi): We rolled in four hundred years ago. / Does that not make us Baekje by now?
[29] D(eldersatek): Four hundred years rolling in. Four hundred rolling out.
[30] D(elderyunbi): Satek is a house that lives by holding the king’s sleeve. / We do not hold the sleeve. We hold the arm.
[31] p: Neither house has ever won, and nothing about that is accidental: the throne needs both of them standing. A clan with no rival starts watching the throne.
[32] p: The rivalry has a quieter register, too — the kind that never makes the street. Each house keeps a clerk in the other’s counting-room. Each house denies it. Every third Assembly, someone finds a cup under a floorboard that was not there when the session opened, and both sides pretend to be shocked.
[33] D(undefined): They say Yunbi already knows what was said in the Satek meeting. / And Satek already knows the Yunbi one. / So both know, and both pretend not to. / That’s politics.
[34] p: Once, both houses secretly agreed to kill a grain levy. It came to the Assembly anyway. The votes lined up as counted. Then Elder Satek, who had nodded all morning, turned his thumb down at the last call. The levy died. Yunbi's men stared. His own men stared harder. He never explained.
[35] cite: 👑 King Mu (71)
[36] D(kingmu): Lord Yunbi… an honour to— / Lord Satek… a new—
[37] D(euija): Father… I have no interest in these clan quarrels. / A king should be for the country—
[38] D(kingmu): My child… learn their names anyway. / …I did not like mine either. I still say them first.
[39] p: “Restore the reign of the thirteenth Eraha!” Every house in Sabi still chants it. To hear why, we go back three hundred years…!

##### samhan › Gunchogo, the 13th (371)
[0] p: Baekje’s thirteenth king marches north to Pyongyang. A Goguryeo king dies on his own wall. In seven hundred years, it never happens again.
[1] p: Baekje has the river, the coast and the sea roads east. The clans take the docks. The throne takes a cut. It is the richest kingdom in Samhan, and the strongest. Neither lasts.
[2] D(nation-baekje): Restore the reign of the thirteenth Eraha.
[3] p: They will still be chanting that sentence three centuries later, in a courtyard, to a clever king who has already decided that a country is a story. It is the sentence that gets Daeya burned.
[4] p: Goguryeo remembers it too, and differently, and for exactly as long.
[5] p: Back to the snow, and to Goguryeo’s most frightening commander. First question: do you know what happens to traitors…?

##### samhan › Commander Yeon (634)
[0] p: In the high mountains of Manchuria, a young man is caught in the snow by a Goguryeo soldier.
[1] p: He is taken to the outpost of Commander Yeon (29), the Eternal General — a ruthless military general.
[2] D(gesomun): Do you know what happens to traitors, young man...?
[3] p: It is over quickly, and it is not clean. Nobody in the yard looks away, because looking away is also a report.
[4] p: The guards talk about him the way men talk about weather. “He’s a monster, you know. Out here they call him the Red Sun of Pyongyang. He’s made the Eastern Commandery the safest in the kingdom. The barbarians run if they hear his name.”
[5] p: The outpost is also a building site. Three summers ago, the Tang flattened Goguryeo's pile of enemy bones. Goguryeo got the message. Now it builds a wall. A thousand li of it. When Yeon isn't killing anybody, he walks it with a plumb line and kicks the crooked stones.
[6] D(gesomun): They say you… leaked our secrets to the enemy. / Do you know what punishment is given to a traitor?
[7] D(undefined): I have… no name.
[8] D(gesomun): Of course. The barbarians always show more respect.
[9] p: A month before the Summit, in a Mohe village the Eastern Command has finished with, there is a boy who will not move out of the doorway of a house that no longer has a roof. Snow is settling on the ash. He has a shaved crown and two braids, and he holds a stick the way he has seen men hold spears. Yeon gets down off the red bay and walks up until the stick touches his chest.
[10] D(gesomun): Move.
[11] D(gulgul): …
[12] D(gesomun): Do you understand me.
[13] D(gulgul): …
[14] p: He does not. Yeon looks at him for what his officers later agree was an unreasonable length of time. Then he laughs, the slap of a laugh they will learn to dread, and pulls off his gloves.
[15] D(gesomun): Look at this one. Guarding a house that’s already burned. / Good. This is what Goguryeo looks like. / Get on. The second horse.
[16] p: He hands the gloves down. They do not fit. The boy gets on the second horse anyway, the stick still in his fist.
[17] D(dosuryu): …You are taking him?
[18] D(gesomun): Where do you think that boy is standing when he is grown.
[19] D(dosuryu): …Opposite us, I should think.
[20] D(gesomun): That is why I am taking him.
[21] p: He gives him the name Gulgul, which is not a Goguryeo name and is not a Mohe one either, and raises him in Pyongyang alongside his own sons — one step behind them at every meal.
[22] p: Years later, on the north wall of Pyongyang in a winter worse than this one, Yeon stands with the grown boy a step behind him and the river frozen white below. He says the thing he says every winter, to anyone in earshot, as if the cold might forget it otherwise.
[23] D(gesomun): Cold?
[24] D(gulgul): …No, sir.
[25] D(gesomun): Liar. I’m cold too. / Remember it anyway. Kings die, courts get tired, walls come down— / <b>Goguryeo never dies.</b>
[26] p: Gulgul grows up quiet. When Yeon sends him to guard the northern marches, he gives him a surname. Dae. Big, as big as the country. Dae Gulgul watches that border for thirty years, and nobody writes down anything else about him. They write a great deal about his son.
[27] p: The summons isn't addressed to him. It's addressed to his father, who still holds the Eastern seal. Yeon Taejo sat in the capital's big chair for twelve years. Now he is too old to ride that far. The son has done the work for years. The seal is still the old man's.
[28] D(yeontaejo): Take the seal. You sit in my place this year. / …And say half of what you think.
[29] D(gesomun): Me? Why do I have to go to Pyongyang? / It’s a place where mouths open only to say useless things…
[30] D(yeontaejo): I know. I sat in it for twelve years. / Half, son. Half.
[31] p: He promised his father half. He has never said half of anything. Next stop: Pyongyang, and a room full of men counting grain…!

##### samhan › High Summit (634)
[0] p: So Yeon rides to Pyongyang in his father's place. Five commanders, one king, one room. They call it the High Summit.
[1] p: He rides in at the red two-tier gate. Pyongyang already knows the sound of those hooves.
[2] p: Goguryeo works like this. Five commanders argue. The High Commander holds the first sword. The king has the last word.
[3] diagram: The High Summit · 제가회의
[4] table: {"kind":"table","head":["King 王","Central Cmd","Northern Cmd","Southern Cmd","Eastern Cmd","Western Cmd"],"rows":[["Yeongnyu (51) 영류왕","Yeon Gusesa (52)","Go Ul (44)","Son Daeha (47)","Yeon Gesomun (2
[5] p: The chamber is already loud when Yeon arrives — not with strategy, with arithmetic. Every banner wants a larger share of the same winter grain.
[6] D(yeongnyu): Enough. / I did not call five commands to Pyongyang to divide a granary. / I will be the “King for All” — Samhan under one roof. Silla and Baekje first.
[7] D(southcmd): Then the Southern Command takes the next levy. / Yushin’s banners have been testing the passes. If His Majesty wants Samhan, give me men — not speeches.
[8] D(northcmd): And leave the north bare? / The Mohe burned three villages last frost — Haemosu’s sun does not reach the north in winter, and neither do Central’s warehouses. I need the cavalry remounts promised at the last Summit.
[9] D(westcmd): The Liao watch needs timber and iron, not another southern adventure. / If we strip the west to chase Samhan, we gift the Tang a road.
[10] D(gusesa): (mild, as if chairing a feast) / Each front believes it is the only front. That is why we meet. / Eastern Command has kept the marches quiet. Let us not reward noise over results.
[11] D(westcmd): My grandfather still toasts Ulchi at the Colossal River — Salsu, the old men say — as if a drowned Sui host were a harvest. / Ansi’s walls are not a toast. They are a bill we keep paying in stone.
[12] D(gesomun): Then stop paying the West in gold for another quiet decade. / Rivers remember who feeds them. So do fortresses.
[13] D(gesomun): Quiet? / I have been killing tribes so this room can argue about who gets the horses. / Meanwhile the Second Emperor — Li Shimin — is not a tribute account. He is a man who murders brothers for a throne and then invents a reason.
[14] D(yeongnyu): Commander Yeon. Watch your tongue about foreign kings. / We have bought decades with gold. We will buy more — and spend the peace on Samhan.
[15] D(gesomun): You cannot buy a man who has already decided the price of your head. / I have watched how courts die: they starve the wall that is screaming, and fatten the wall that flatters. / Give the west grain. Give the north horses. Give the south whatever fairy tale you like — / but do not sit here pretending the Second Emperor is a weather we can ignore because tribute is habit.
[16] D(southcmd): Easy for the East to lecture. You fight people without cities. / I fight Kim Yushin. Send me the next levy or stop talking about Samhan.
[17] D(northcmd): And I will not freeze another winter while Central counts my remounts twice.
[18] D(westcmd): Nor will I strip the Liao for a king’s poem about one peninsula.
[19] p: Yeon’s hands are flat on the table. The nails have gone white. This is the face of a man who has already fought the war the room refuses to schedule.
[20] D(gesomun): Listen to yourselves. / Horses. Timber. Bodies. A crown-word. / When the Second Emperor comes he will not ask which of you was most polite in committee.
[21] D(gusesa): If you keep defying the king, Commander Yeon… / we may have to name you a traitor.
[22] D(gusesa): (to Yeon, almost kindly — which is worse) / Nephew. Sit down. The Summit does not run on prophecies.
[23] D(gesomun): …. / Then keep your Summit. / Keep your tribute. Keep your Samhan dream carved into a budget fight. / When the Second Emperor’s drums reach the Liao, remember who tried to spoil the feast.
[24] p: He walks out before it ends. Outside, the corridor is very long and very cold. Behind him the chamber returns to numbers — as if he had never brought an emperor into the room.
[25] D(gesomun): Heaven above… help this foolish country…!
[26] p: In the yard the Eastern banners answer him anyway — a roar that has nothing to do with the Summit’s minutes.
[27] D(dosuryu): Look at that — see how Pyongyang loves you.
[28] D(gesomun): Of course. The people have never once abandoned me. / It is the politicians…!
[29] D(gesomun): His Majesty wants Samhan under one roof. / The Summit wants the roof itemised. / …Get the horses. I would rather sleep in a tent tonight.
[30] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"Birth of Namseng","ko":"남생의 탄생"}
[31] p: Yeon’s wife labours in a Goguryeo timber chamber blasted white with daylight — no extra bodies, no portrait-frame crowd. Only the midwife who opens a birth, and the mother. The rest of the world falls out of the light.
[32] D(yeonwife): Samsin… / This child alone — please. / …This time — please.
[33] p: The portrait does not stay paint. Samsin steps from the frame the way steam steps from a kettle — one midwife of the living world under Little Star — and lays a hand where mortal hands have failed.
[34] D(samsin): Do not weep. / I will open the breath. / The name — that is yours to give.
[35] p: So the first heir arrives under Samsin's hand, the year of the Summit. They call him Namseng. A son is born. Nobody wanted a poem in the name. It's the sound the room makes when the baby breathes.
[36] D(gesomun): Namseng. / …Heavier than it sounds. / This country. You will have to keep it.
[37] p: Once, Goguryeo did not argue about grain. It had a king with sixty-four fortresses. To meet him, we go back two centuries…!

##### samhan › Gwanggaeto, the Great King (400)
[0] p: Silla is drowning. An army from across the sea is inside its walls. Then Gwanggaeto sends fifty thousand horsemen south, and the Wa are gone.
[1] p: A red sun. The three-legged crow rides south on his banners. The stele will list sixty-four fortresses. It will not list the nerve it took.
[2] p: Sixty-four fortresses, one reign. The stele at his tomb lists them all.
[3] map: {"kind":"map","from":391,"year":412,"places":["gungnae","surabol","geumgwan"],"caption":"Watch the red run south. One reign did that.","ko":"붉은빛이 남쪽으로 번지는 걸 보라. 한 사람의 치세가 한 일이다."}
[4] p: Silla had asked. That's the part everyone forgets. A Silla king, with foreigners inside his capital, sent north and begged. Fifty thousand horsemen came down and cleared the peninsula. Then they didn't leave for fifty years.
[5] D(herald): They did save us.
[6] D(herald): So why are they still here?
[7] p: Silla’s crown princes go north as hostages. Silla’s court takes Goguryeo titles. Silla’s army takes Goguryeo orders. It lasts two generations. Silla does not forget it.
[8] p: Two hundred and forty years later a Silla prince will stand in front of a foreign emperor and ask for an army, and every single person in Surabol will know exactly what that costs, because it has been done to them before.
[9] QUOTE: 庶寧其業 國富民殷 五穀豊熟 || The common people were at peace in their work; the country was rich and the people abundant; the five grains ripened in plenty. || Gwanggaeto Stele (廣開土王碑), south face, ll. 3–4 (414 CE); Best, “The Kwanggaeto Stele,” p. 147
[10] p: Bupmin is fifteen now. The Hwarang have five rules, and his uncle has one question: which will you break first…?

##### five-principles › Bupmin (641)
[0] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"Flowering Youth","ko":"화랑의 꽃"}
[1] p: It is the spring Bupmin turns fifteen.
[2] p: The Hwarang train under the Marshal: horse, bow, verse, and above all gyuku, a horse-ball game a lazier age will call polo.
[3] p: Bupmin (15) is old enough for the headband and too young to invent a country alone. His father is in the Council chamber collecting votes. His uncle keeps the yard.
[4] diagram: Yard as state · 화랑
[5] p: Yushin does not soften the yard because the boy is royal. He softens nothing. The new boys sleep six to a hall and learn each other's snores before each other's ranks. They trade rumours about the Marshal like relics. He took forty fortresses. He bathes in a haunted lake. He can hear a lie drop a shoulder at fifty paces.
[6] p: Girls crowd the fence of the yard the way other towns crowd a market — not for the ball, for the Hwarang. They pretend they came for the verse.
[7] p: Nobody in Surabol would dream of calling gyuku a pastime — it is a ranking system with horses, and a boy’s seat among the Hwarang is half his blood and half his swing. Handicaps are argued the way ministers argue borders, only with less honesty.
[8] p: Then there are the clubs. A premium gyuku club is not a stick. Third-growth cypress from the south ridge of Namsan, seasoned seven years in the shade of Hwangnyong, the grip wrapped in indigo the Queen’s seamstresses will not sell. The head travels in its own box. If you cannot name the forest, you are not asked back.
[9] D(herald): That club — Gaya ironwood core? / No — Wolseong cypress. Last season’s. / …Last season? And he brought it out?
[10] D(alchun): A True Bone does not play last season’s shaft. / Is that law? / Worse.
[11] D(yushin): Again. / A king for all who cannot hold a saddle is a poem, not a country.
[12] D(munmu): Uncle— / I said that when I was six.
[13] D(yushin): Then make it true at fifteen. / The Hwarang do not train for your father’s cleverness. They train for the hour the cleverness runs out.
[14] D(yushin): We ride the eastern practice roads until the Fortress of Radiance looks small behind us. / Westward, Baekje’s Yellow Mountain pass is where their grain carts complain in dry weeks — learn a landscape before it learns your name.
[15] p: The Hwarang follow a set of Five Principles.
[16] verse: {"kind":"verse","color":"#dc2626","lines":["사군이충 (事君以忠): 충성으로 임금을 섬긴다.","사친이효 (事親以孝): 효도로써 부모를 섬긴다.","교우이신 (交友以信): 믿음으로써 벗을 사귄다.","임전무퇴 (臨戰無退): 전쟁에 나가 물러서지 않는다.","살생유택 (殺生有擇): 살아있는 것을 죽일 때에는 가림이 있어야 한
[17] p: At dusk he gathers the flower youth under the eaves and speaks the Five Principles the way other houses recite ancestors — not as decoration, but as the only map that still works when bone rank fails. The boys mouth the words along with him, elbowing each other at no retreat, going quiet at no needless killing, each privately certain the Marshal is looking straight at him. He is looking at all of them.
[18] D(yushin): Loyalty to the sovereign. / Filial duty to parents. / Trust among friends. / No retreat in battle. / No needless killing. / Bupmin — which one will you break first?
[19] D(munmu): …Retreat. / When Gotaso rides too fast I always pull up first. Every time. / If I am to be a king for all, I cannot be the boy who only follows.
[20] D(yushin): Good. / Then see the country the way a Hwarang sees a field — who holds, who falters, who dies for a vow they meant. / I am marshal of this order. You will learn loyalty here before you learn how to sit on a throne.
[21] p: The yard has two names it still whispers. Tonight the Marshal says them out loud…!

##### five-principles › Gotaso (641)
[0] p: A young girl is going to do what she’s going to do.

##### five-principles › Pumsuk (641)
[0] p: Princess Gotaso (16) has fallen in love with the Hwarang Pumsuk (23), and the whole court can see it before either of them admits the word. The maids keep score of the accidental meetings. Which is why the wine is late.

##### five-principles › Munhee (625)
[0] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"How They Met","ko":"첫 만남"}
[1] D(chunchu): Dear… have you already forgotten how we met?
[2] p: It starts with a dream, and the dream is sold.
[3] D(bohee): Last night… I climbed Namsan and I relieved myself, / and all of Surabol drowned. / The entire capital.
[4] D(munhee): Sister. Sell me that dream.
[5] D(bohee): …For what?
[6] D(munhee): My silk skirt.
[7] p: Bohee takes the skirt. It is the single worst trade in Silla’s thousand years, and the two of them will both live long enough to know it.
[8] D(munhee): The capital you drowned / is mine now.
[9] p: Five days later Yushin brings a young nobleman home from the gyuku field — still dusty, still arguing about a disputed foul — and on the yard, mid-demonstration of a “proper True Bone grip,” steps on the hem of the man’s coat on purpose. The tie comes away.
[10] D(yushin): Oh dear. / My apologies. / Somebody sew that for the gentleman.
[11] D(bohee): …How could I approach a nobleman over so small a thing.

[13] p: He has to take the coat off for her to mend it. Magenta silk leaves his shoulders. He sits disrobed in her brother’s hall with a True Bone’s embarrassment and nowhere to put his hands. She knits the tear standing close enough to feel the heat off his skin — and that is all, the first time. Needle. Breath. The slow fact of a man without his coat.
[14] D(chunchu): …Your hands are quick. / I have… not sat like this.

[16] p: He comes back the next day, needing nothing sewn, and again the day after that. Each visit she finds a new place on the garment — and they sit closer. The needle slows. His breath learns the back of her hand. They do not leap. They accumulate.
[17] p: On a later visit the coat is off again. She stands behind him, needle forgotten, staring at the breadth of his shoulders as if the knitting were only an excuse to keep looking. Magenta silk has slipped. She does not tell him to cover it. When the needle pauses it is because her mouth has found the place above his pulse — and Yushin is careful to be looking somewhere else the entire time.

[19] D(munhee): Because you have not left yet. / Before you leave… / your hand belongs at my waist. / Until the sewing is done.

[45] p: Chunchu &amp; Munhee are married — the burnt-skirt rumour becomes a wedding, and the wedding becomes a household that is openly fond of itself.
[46] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"The Closed Months","ko":"닫힌 달들"}
[47] p: The wedding itself is quiet. Magenta silk and pink silk share a cup. What the court will later call a clever match is, in the room, simply two adults who have already learned each other’s breath.
[48] p: They shut the door on the yard and do not open it again for a long time. The minutes will later invent one decorous wedding night. What actually happens is weeks of it — her on him, him on her, the magenta and the pink in a heap by the door — until the meals go cold and Surabol learns to wait.
[49] p: The first time he is still trying to be gentle. She is not. She takes his hand and puts it where she wants it, and the sound that leaves her is not a toast. He lasts like a man who has been polite too long, which is to say not long, and says her name at the end as if he were apologising for it. She laughs, because that was the point, and does not let him go anywhere. The bedding. The chest. The floor, when the bedding is too far away. When he reaches for the water jug she pulls him back by the wrist.
[50] D(munhee): Again…? / Today… don’t even try to count. / Save counting for outside.
[51] D(chunchu): I… cannot count. / Munhee. / I have… already lost. / And… I will lose again.
[52] p: For weeks they do not leave the bedding except to drink, to laugh, to start again. She wakes with him still beside her and starts again before the laugh is finished. She rides him until her thighs shake and asks for more the way she would ask for a sum he is good at. A strategist who can forecast a betrayal a generation out cannot forecast his own stamina, and does not care.
[53] p: The neighbors on both walls learn their names the wrong way — through plaster, through 다시, through a rhythm that does not stop when the lamp does. Servants stop knocking. Someone on the east side moves a sleeping mat farther from the shared timber and blames the draft.
[54] p: At night the courtyard looks up and learns worse. The paper window glows — warm lamp inside, blue-black street outside — and on the 창호지 the shadows are unmistakable: one figure straddling the other; two bodies pressed to the lattice; upright, tangled, a lift that makes a silhouette into a confession. No faces needed. The pose is the gossip.
[55] p: A neighbor freezes mid-step under the eaves, looks up at the shadow on the lattice, and looks away too late. By the third night half the lane has an opinion, and none of it is about politics.
[56] D(munhee): They say… they heard us through the wall. / And saw… the paper window. / Even our names.
[57] D(chunchu): Then the wall… is on our side. / And the paper window. / If Surabol hears… / let it.
[58] p: They fit. Not the polite fit of a well-arranged marriage: when he is all the way with her she makes a noise like someone who has been waiting years for exactly that, and then laughs into it, because he is already moving again. Neither pretends to be shy. Later the household will call it love, which is also true. In the bed she only says again, and don’t you dare stop.
[59] p: Morning finds them still tangled — lattice light on flushed faces, her thigh over his hip, the pink silk she never put back on crumpled under them. He wants her again before he is properly awake. She laughs into his mouth and lets him, slowly this time, which is somehow worse. He kisses the place above her pulse the way she once kissed his. The strategist’s cleverness has nowhere to go but her.
[60] D(munhee): Dear. / Outside… later. / For now, count only me.
[61] D(chunchu): That… / is the one sum I am good at.
[62] p: Months pass before either of them remembers the yard. When they finally open the door she walks like someone who has been thoroughly loved and does not mind the lane knowing it, and they look at each other like people who have won a private war — still in love, still hungry, and willing, for one afternoon, to put clothes back on.
[63] p: When they reappear, the marriage is already a fact the city has stopped gossiping about — replaced by the quieter envy of people who heard the walls, saw the glowing lattice, and wished their own houses were that lucky.

[66] p: Years later the same house keeps a different quiet. Munhee holds the boy against her collarbone. They will call him Bupmin. [67] p: The household fills with Bupmin, who walks early, and Gotaso, who talks early and never stops.

##### five-principles › Grand Academy (641)
[0] p: Yeon's wife has given him three sons. They could not be more different.
[1] p: Namseng (7) is the careful one — the heir, eager to be approved of.
[2] p: Namgun (4) is the fierce one, who never backs down first.
[3] p: Namsan (2) is the quiet one, watching his brothers.
[4] p: There is a fourth boy at that table who is not counted, because counting him would require a word nobody in the house wants to use. Gulgul eats after the others and says nothing, and Namsan — who watches everything — is the only one who notices that he never sits with his back to a door.
[5] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"The Taehak","ko":"태학"}
[6] p: The Grand Academy is old. It came over the river in the same season as the first Buddhas. Ever since, the school and the temple have shared Goguryeo's noble sons. Classics in the morning. Sutras after lunch. Archery whenever the masters lose their voices.
[7] p: Yeon brings Namseng (7) to the gate himself, in riding boots, and does not take them off on the swept stone.
[8] D(undefined): Commander. The sons of the five commanderies begin with the Analects and the Lotus Sutra. / As your own father did, if I remember the register.
[9] D(gesomun): The Analects, fine. A boy should know how to bow before he decides not to. / The sutra he can skip.
[10] D(namseng): Father. / Is the Buddha not allowed?
[11] D(gesomun): The Buddha’s fine. Fat, quiet, never asked me for anything. / It’s his landlords I mind.
[12] p: The landlords are not a figure of speech. Half the good valley land belongs to monasteries. The monasteries belong to the great houses whose second sons run them. None of it pays for the wall. Every spring Yeon writes to the Summit about this. Every spring the Summit thanks him for his piety.
[13] p: What he wants instead is the Way of Laozi, which is an odd thing for him to want, because the Tang emperors claim Laozi as their ancestor. Yeon has heard this and does not care. He has a sentence for it, the only one he ever repeats word for word.
[14] D(gesomun): A pot stands on three legs. / Confucius is one. The Buddha’s two. We’re missing the third, and the pot’s tipping into the fire.
[15] D(undefined): The third leg would be… Tang priests, Commander?
[16] D(gesomun): The third leg is whatever doesn’t own a farm.
[17] p: Across the courtyard a monk named Bodeok has stopped sweeping. He is from the monastery at Banryong, which owns a great deal of farm, and he will remember the sentence longer than anyone else who hears it.
[18] p: The complaint reaches the High Commander’s table before Yeon has ridden home. Gusesa reads it at supper, between courses.
[19] D(gusesa): (mild, wiping his fingers) A Yeon telling monks what to own. / My nephew collects enemies the way other men collect horses. At least horses eat less.
[20] p: Namseng is enrolled anyway. He learns the Analects first and best, and on the days the sutra master is ill he reads his father’s copy of the Daodejing, which has never been opened past the first page.
[21] p: Field trip. Yeon takes the boys to see a very big rock. The rock has a list on it, and a question…!

##### five-principles › King Euija (641)
[0] p: King Mu is dead at eighty, after a lifetime of fighting Silla.

##### five-principles › Yunchung (641)
[0] p: There was only one man Euija knew he could trust to deliver.
[1] p: That winter Euija sends for Yunchung, and nobody from the eight houses is told. Yunchung is a general from a family too small to keep a clan tutor. He has held the Silla frontier for eleven years by doing exactly what he says he will do, which the Assembly finds tiring.
[2] D(euija): Sit, General. No, the good cushion. Take it before I change my mind. / Tell me. Who rules Baekje?
[3] D(yunchung): Your Majesty does. / On paper.
[4] D(euija): Ha! And off paper?
[5] D(yunchung): Off paper, the Rock does. And whoever rubs the brine on it. / The eight houses pick the Premier, the Premier picks the ministers, and the ministers send me the grain late. They pay my men. My men know it.
[6] D(euija): So. How does a king get his country back off the Rock without a war at home?
[7] D(yunchung): With a war abroad, Majesty. / A king who wins a fortress owns the men who took it. The clans can’t vote on a victory. They can only show up to the feast.
[8] D(euija): Plainly put. / I like a man who says the ugly thing without a cushion under it. Even when he’s sitting on mine.
[9] p: It is the first time in the reign that Euija says what he has decided before the Assembly hears it. By spring the Assembly will hear it anyway, in the form of a question he has already answered.
[10] p: That winter, the Assembly's loud fight isn't about war. It's about a shipping writ. A Satek cousin has died without a son, and somebody has to inherit the salt, the iron and the run to the islands. Gyebek sits through three sessions. He understands every number and none of the smiles.
[11] D(ministersatek): The writ stays in the house. / A harbour that changes clans mid-monsoon is how grain rots in the hold.
[12] D(elderyunbi): Then say clan, not country. / We are tired of hearing harbour when you mean Satek.
[13] D(euija): Enough. / When the frontier is settled, you may resume counting berths. / Until then — the Eraha counts fortresses.
[14] p: Euija has already decided. Now the clans have to believe it was their idea.
[15] p: The Premier is chosen via the Rock of Politics — a ritual the Great Clans have controlled for generations.
[16] diagram: Rock of Politics · 정사암
[17] D(chunbok): As Your Majesty well knows, / the will of the Rock is the will of Heaven. / The eight houses decide it together.
[18] D(euija): Heaven…? Ah — the invisible committee. / Spirits and gods — the cheapest civil servants. / They never ask for berths, they never read the ledger, and the people kneel without being told twice.
[19] D(nation-baekje): Restore the reign of the thirteenth Eraha…! / The thirteenth Eraha…! Ten thousand years!
[20] D(euija): Ah… in Silla, they worship the Cloud King like a god. / Do you know what kind of man the Cloud King was…?
[21] D(euija): He signed an alliance with us, and then he took the river. / Surabol carved him four stones for it.
[22] D(euija): Do you know what a country is? / <b>A country is a territory governed by a single story.</b> / Why are we Baekje people, and not Goryeo or Silla people? We look exactly the same. / Anywhere in Baekje, everyone knows the founders. / Speak of King Onjo — that is Baekje. / So the king makes the story. / Let us make an interesting one…!
[23] D(euija): Goryeo is too large to move. / Silla is too old to surprise anybody.
[24] D(chunbok): The present king of Silla is a woman who cannot command an army, / and even within her country, the people’s hearts are unsettled. / Seize this opening, take a border fortress, and the great work will be within reach.
[25] D(seongchung): Your Majesty — is this the country you mean to hand the princes?
[26] D(euija): No, Gyebek… not you. / Why use an ox-cleaver to kill a chicken?
[27] D(gyebek): Your Majesty. Does that mean you will not use me, or that you are saving me?
[28] D(euija): …It means I am saving you.
[29] D(gyebek): Then say that. I do not follow figures of speech.
[30] p: The Assembly finds him rude, which misses the point by a courtyard’s width. All he wants — every single time — is the sentence handed over with nothing folded inside it, and nobody at that court has spoken that way in their lives.

##### five-principles › The Severing (553–554)
[0] p: The sad thing about betrayal… is that it never comes from your enemies.
[1] p: Two kings take a river back together. One is Seong of Baekje. The other is the Cloud King. The deal is simple. Baekje gets the river mouth, near the sea. Silla gets the upper valley.
[2] p: For a while the two banners still fly side by side. Then the Cloud King turns his army on Baekje's half. He takes the river mouth and gives it a new name. He fills it with men who won't ask what the alliance meant.

[20] QUOTE: 新羅謂佐知村飼馬奴苦都 更名谷智 曰 苦都賤奴也 明王名主也 今使賤奴殺名主 冀傳後世 莫忘於口 已而苦都乃獲明王 再拜曰 請斬王首 明王對曰 王頭不合受奴手 苦都曰 我國法 違背所盟 雖曰國王 當受奴手 明王乘踞胡床 解授佩刀於谷知令斬 明王仰天大息涕泣 許諾曰 寡人每念 常痛入骨髓 顧計不可苟活 乃延首受斬 苦都斬首而殺 新羅留理明王頭骨 而以禮送餘骨於百濟 今新羅王埋明王骨於北廳階下 名此廳曰都堂 || Silla told Kodo, a horse-tending slave of Sajichon, renamed Gokji: Kodo is a low slave and King Seong a lord with a name; have the slave kill the lord, so later ages will hear it and not forget it in the mouth. Kodo captured the king, bowed twice, and said, Let me cut off the king’s head. The king answered, A king’s head should not receive a slave’s hand. Kodo said, By our law, if one breaks a sworn alliance, even a king receives a slave’s hand. The king sat on a camp stool, unfastened his own sword, and gave it to Gokji to cut with. He looked up to heaven, sighed loud, wept, and consented: Whenever I think of it, the pain has always reached the marrow. Reckoning it, I cannot live on in disgrace. Then he stretched out his neck and received the cut. Kodo cut off the head and killed him. Silla kept the skull and sent the rest of the bones to Baekje with rite. The Silla king buried the bone under the steps of the north hall, and named that hall the capital court. || Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 19, Emperor Kinmei, yr. 15 (554), 12th month — the killing of King Seong (明王); Aston tr., vol. 2

##### iron-will › Yeon’s Massacre (642)
[0] p: Yeon's father dies in the spring, in his own bed in the east. The seal should pass to the son. The Summit takes the whole summer to admit it. When it finally does, Yeon decides to host a banquet. The king is in attendance.
[1] p: All summer he has bowed. He went to every seat at the Summit one at a time and asked for his father’s seal like a younger son asking for an inheritance. Among themselves they have already agreed that he will have it for one winter, out on the border forts, and not come back.
[2] p: October cold sits under the eaves. The lamps are already lit when the Five Commanderies take their seats — wine first, then meat, then the old joke that Pyongyang never runs out of either. Each commander wears a ring-pommel sword at his hip, the three-legged crow stamped in the ring. The hall smells of sesame oil and autumn horse-sweat brought in on Eastern boots.
[3] D(yeongnyu): Ah — so even the renowned Gesomun has learned to bow… / Your father would have liked to see it.
[4] D(yeongnyu): Good — everyone is here. / We settle the succession today.

[8] p: Every door in the hall closes at once, from the outside.
[9] p: The side doors were never for servants. When they open again, Yeon’s soldiers come through every one of them. Tables overturn. Wine becomes a darker color before anyone names it. For hours, blood and tears fill the banquet hall as hundreds of officials and generals are killed. Yeon does not shout orders — he walks the length of the room the way a man walks a border he has already decided to keep, and he takes each commander’s blade himself.
[10] p: First the Southern Commander. He wanted the next levy for Yushin’s passes, and called Eastern fighting easy work.

[30] p: He finally approaches King Youngryu for the final blow. The crown has slid. The Samhan dream is still in the king’s mouth, too late to be a budget.

[34] p: He steps into the doorway with the blades on his back. Red-wing chalgap fills the door.
[35] D(gesomun): Loyal men of Goguryeo — hear the words of Yeon Gesomun! / In the south, Baekje and Silla covet us, / and in the west the Second Emperor comes this way, butchering nation after nation! / And all the while an incompetent king and rotten ministers shut their eyes to the world and lead this country down the road to ruin!! / Silla and the East, then Baekje the next day, then the Tang!
[36] D(gesomun): But what of the people? We have nowhere else to go! / We live on this land, we die on it, and we are the ones who bleed every time they come! / The world will call us mad! Of course — to take your own fate in your own hands has always looked like madness to the world!

[61] p: The capital learns a new etiquette. Remaining officials swear loyalty not to the nephew-king’s smile but to the Supreme Commander’s door. Men who hesitate are removed before winter — titles stripped, names scratched from the rolls, a few bodies found where the river turns. The foreign hostels lock from the outside. Tribute missions that once bought another quiet decade are cancelled mid-packing; silk meant for Chang’an stays in the warehouses.
[62] p: March boots outrank court shoes. Drums outrank flutes. Monks keep their heads down while the new Taoist masters walk the halls Yeon starved of incense. Envoys who still ask for audience are told the kingdom is closed for inventory — of grain, of blades, of who belongs inside the walls. Goguryeo under Yeon watches the roads in and trusts almost none of them.

[33] D(euija): We have our own mouth — the White River under Sabi. / Clan berths stacked like teeth. Cut Danghangseong and Silla starves for partners; keep our river and we eat either way.
[34] D(gesomun): You sound like a harbour clerk. / Good. Kings who forget docks start wars they cannot feed.
[35] D(gesomun): Do you know a “Kim Chunchu” of Silla?
[36] D(euija): Kim Chunchu? First I have heard of him… royalty? Why?
[37] D(gesomun): Just… curious. He does not seem to care for you much. / He spoke of being rid of you, hands folded in prayer.
[38] D(euija): Chunchu… whoever he is, a man who stores things up like that is no easy sort. / But I do not fear a man who kneels to others.
[39] p: For a moment Yeon’s eyes go somewhere else — to a door, to a hand, to a stare that did not ask to be liked.
[40] flashback: the hand
[41] D(gesomun): That Chunchu… / He put steel through his own hand to make me listen. / I have met one other man with eyes like that.
[42] D(euija): Oh?
[43] D(gesomun): You. / I do not yet know which of you frightens me more.
[44] D(euija): Flattery. Keep going.
[45] D(gesomun): It was not flattery.
[46] D(gesomun): You came with three. You’re leaving with five. / …Did Your Majesty come as an envoy, or to do some shopping?
[47] D(euija): I have a gift for gathering people. You have a gift for reducing them.
[48] D(courtmaid): Your Majesty. Goryeo is cold. / Shall we… warm you?
[49] D(courtmaid): With mouths. With thighs. / Even while you look at the map.
[50] D(euija): I am aware. / …Both of you, come. / Quietly. / Before Commander Yeon… hears.
[51] D(courtmaid): So tonight two of us will come in.
[52] D(courtmaid): One body isn’t enough… to hold Your Majesty. / From both sides… at once.
[53] D(euija): …Don’t flatter.
[54] D(euija): The body… is already answering.
[55] D(courtmaid): It isn’t flattery.
[56] D(courtmaid): The hands… remember. / Where Your Majesty… told them to go last night.
[57] p: In the morning he rides south with all five. Nobody raises the subject of the extra two. He carries a map of Danghangseong in his head, and Yeon’s warning about Chunchu folded away like a knife he intends to use later.
[58] p: Why does the Eternal General flinch at one Silla name? Go back to a ditch, a white horse, and an unknown captain…!

##### iron-will › Nangbi (629)
[0] p: Kim Yushin — a name that strikes fear in all of Samhan. Maybe this is why.
[1] p: Autumn. Silla’s army is breaking against a Goguryeo wall. The men who should be charging are sitting in the trenches. Yushin is thirty-four, a banner captain. His white horse doesn’t even have a name.
[2] QUOTE: 建福四十六年己丑秋八月 王遣伊湌任末里 波珍湌龍春白龍 蘇判大因舒玄等 率兵攻高句麗娘臂城 麗人出兵逆擊之 吾人失利 死者衆多 衆心折衄 無復鬪心 || In the eighth month of autumn, in the forty-sixth year of Geonbok, a gichuk year, the king sent the Ichan Im Malli, the Pajinchan Yongchun and Baekryong, and the Sopan Daein and Seohyeon at the head of an army to attack the Goguryeo fortress of Nangbi. The Goguryeo men came out and struck back without warning. Our side was beaten and many died; the men’s spirit was broken, and they had no heart left to fight. || Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2 (Nangbi Fortress, 629)
[3] p: He rides back to his father’s command post, gets down, and takes off his helmet, which is how a son asks permission in front of an army.
[4] D(yushin): Father. We’re losing. / They say you shake a coat by the collar to make it hang straight, and lift the head-rope to open a net. / …Let me be the collar.
[5] D(seohyeon): …Put your helmet on. / Then go.
[6] QUOTE: 庾信時爲中幢幢主 進於父前 脫胄而告曰 我兵敗北 吾平生以忠孝自期 臨戰不可不勇 || Yushin was then captain of the Middle Banner. He went before his father, took off his helmet, and said: “Our army is beaten. All my life I have held myself to loyalty to the country and duty to my parents; facing battle, I cannot fail to be brave.” || Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2 (Nangbi Fortress, 629)
[7] QUOTE: 蓋聞振領而裘正 提綱而網張 吾其爲綱領乎 迺跨馬拔劍 跳坑 出入賊陣 斬將軍 提其首而來 || “I have heard that when you shake the collar the coat hangs straight, and when you lift the head-rope the net opens. Let me be that rope and that collar.” Then he mounted his horse, drew his sword, leapt the trench, and went in and out of the enemy lines; he cut down their general and came back carrying his head. || Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2 (Nangbi Fortress, 629)
[8] p: The white horse takes the trench in one jump that the men in it will describe for the rest of their lives, usually with their hands. In, out. In again. The third time Yushin comes back there is something heavy hanging from his saddle, and the men in the trench are already climbing out.
[9] QUOTE: 乃跨馬拔劒 向敵陣直前 三入三出 每入或斬將或搴旗 || Then he mounted, drew his sword and rode straight at the enemy line. Three times he went in and three times he came out, and each time he went in he either cut down a commander or tore down a banner. || Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 4, Silla Annals — King Jinpyeong, year 51 (629)
[10] p: He brings the weight on his saddle back to the command post and sets it down in the mud in front of his father, wrapped in a torn banner, because he does not know what else a son is supposed to do with a general’s head. The staff officers wait for the speech. Seohyeon looks at the bundle, then at the boy, for long enough that someone coughs.
[11] D(seohyeon): …Your helmet’s crooked.
[12] p: He reaches up and straightens it himself, both hands, the way you fix a boy’s collar before a feast, and then turns away and shouts for his officers before anyone can see his face. It is the most Kim Seohyeon has ever said to his son about anything, and Yushin will carry it longer than the helmet.
[13] QUOTE: 我軍見之 乘勝奮擊 斬殺五千餘級 生擒一千人 城中兇懼無敢抗 皆出降 || Our soldiers saw it, rode the turn of the battle and threw themselves into the attack. They took more than five thousand heads and a thousand prisoners alive. The people inside the walls were so terrified that none dared resist, and all came out and surrendered. || Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2 (Nangbi Fortress, 629)
[14] p: That night he asks the groom what the white horse is called. The groom says it has no name; it came from the royal stable as a spare. Yushin looks at it for a long time, at the mud on its chest and the way it still will not quite stand still.
[15] D(yushin): Hangyul. / …It means steady. It came back steady. All three times.
[16] p: The few who get out of Nangbi walk north for nine days with the story, and it grows a little at every well. By Pyongyang the white horse has cleared the trench at a gallop with a general’s head in one hand and a banner in the other, and the man on it has a name the Goguryeo clerks must write down for the first time.
[17] QUOTE: 十二年 秋八月 新羅將軍金庾信 來侵東邊 破娘臂城 || Twelfth year, autumn, the eighth month: the Silla general Kim Yushin invaded the eastern border and broke Nangbi Fortress. || Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 20, Goguryeo Annals — King Yeongnyu, year 12 (629)
[18] p: In Pyongyang the report is read to the king twice, the second time because he asks for it. At the back of the hall the Yeon heir, twenty-four, stands with his arms folded, the way he stands everywhere.
[19] D(yeongnyu): Kim Yushin… a banner captain. / We have never heard the name.
[20] D(gesomun): You’ll hear it again. / One man jumps one ditch and five thousand of ours lie down. That’s a captain? That’s a sword. / Silla’s sword.
[21] scene: {"kind":"scene","label":"The High Commander’s House","ko":"막리지의 집"}
[22] p: Gesomun’s family lives in the big house below the palace hill. His father, Yeon Taejo, has run the Summit for ten years. Long enough to outlive most of the men who voted for him. None of the ones who voted against. Most nights he comes home in a silence the servants have learned to walk around.
[23] p: Tonight he does not take off his boots. He sits at the low table with a copy of the Nangbi report, the one the king asked to hear twice, and reads it a third time with his finger under the lines.
[24] D(gesomun): Father. You’re still on that? / It’s one fortress. We take it back by spring.
[25] D(yeontaejo): Sit. / …Five thousand heads. Off one charge. How many men have you seen do that?
[26] D(gesomun): One. / You. At the Colossal River.
[27] D(yeontaejo): I had thirty thousand men and a river on my side. / He had a ditch and a horse.
[28] p: Gesomun has seen his father angry, drunk and bleeding, and once, when he was seven, riding home from the Colossal River with a Sui banner rolled under his arm like a bolt of cloth. He has never seen him frightened of a piece of paper. He finds he does not know where to put his hands.
[29] D(yeontaejo): Thirty-four, and still a banner captain. Silla won’t let a Gaya grandson climb any faster. / They’re wasting him. They won’t waste him forever.
[30] D(gesomun): Then I’ll kill him before they stop.
[31] D(yeontaejo): You’ll try. / Listen to me. Never on a field he picked. Never when you’re angry. And when this city tells you he’s only a captain, don’t believe it.
[32] D(gesomun): His Majesty already did.
[33] D(yeontaejo): His Majesty heard it twice and asked the Summit what to do. / Do you know what the Summit did? Argued half a day over who pays to rebuild the fort. Nobody said his name. Not once. / Ten years I’ve sat in that room. They’ll lose this country one granary at a time and call it caution.
[34] p: Each of them learns his country at home. Euija learns the great clans at his father’s table. Chunchu learns the council from the day it walked his grandfather off the throne. And Gesomun learns this city here, from an old man reading one report three times by lamplight. Nobody else in the city would read it once.
[35] D(gesomun): …Kim Yushin.
[36] p: That’s where the name comes from. Not from his own capital, which likes its titles stamped and filed. From the people he beat. Goguryeo calls him the Sword of Silla first, and means it as a warning. On the border, mothers use it to get children indoors before dark. Thirteen years later, Gesomun will hear that sword is riding for the prince in his prison. He’ll remember a hall, a report read twice, and his father reading it a third time.
[37] p: Thirteen years on, the banner captain has a queen, a title, and a long list of Baekje fortresses. He's working through it…!

##### iron-will › Forty Fortresses (642)
[0] p: In the meantime Queen Sunduk sends her general, Kim Yushin, against Baekje.
[1] D(euija): I-i-it’s Kim Yushin!!
[2] D(euija): You’ve never heard of Kim Yushin…?
[3] D(euija): You fool — Kim Yushin is the Greatest Blade of Samhan…! / Yeon Gesomun, General Gyebek — tell them all to stand aside. Or tell Gyebek the title is still disputed. He will not laugh.
[4] p: Over the next few years Yushin takes more than forty fortresses.
[5] p: In Baekje’s markets they spit when they say his title. At home they toast it. Both sides add, quietly, that Gyebek hasn’t met him yet. Until he does, “greatest blade” is a tavern argument with two right answers.
[6] D(yushin): After the twentieth, nobody was counting.
[7] D(chunchu): And you kept taking them anyway.
[8] D(yushin): …If I stopped, they would invent a reason for my stopping.
[9] p: Between campaigns he still goes alone to the cavern lake. The stone in the story is his father’s. His own pocket is empty. He undresses anyway.
[10] D(narim): You came with a question, or you came because the hill opened. / Either is fine. Sit down before you fall in again. And take the rest off. I want the question from a bare man.
[11] D(yushin): Three things. / The northern door. The queen’s count. How long I may stay.
[12] D(golhwa): Stay is not a number, marshal. / Sit. Unnie will do the other two. I’ll do the one she pretends isn’t counsel.
[13] D(golhwa): It involves my mouth.
[14] p: Hyullé does not speak. She has already warmed the far ledge. Her eyes are on his mouth while Narim answers the north. He will ride before I finish a sentence.
[15] D(narim): Yeon’s door is a guest-door only from one side. / The queen’s count is the one they will not let her finish. Bring her the west in numbers. Do not stand in front of the chair. / Take what you need. Leave before Golhwa asks you to stay. She will ask.
[16] D(narim): She will also try to sit on you. I’m only warning you about one of those.
[17] D(golhwa): Stay. In the water.
[18] D(golhwa): On me, if you can bear the youngest being first.
[19] D(yushin): Guest-door. Numbers. Behind the chair. Leave before stay. / I have the three answers. That is enough.
[20] D(euija): Yushin, my friend~~ / My men stop eating at the sound of your name.
[21] p: One star over Samhan tonight. Three men are looking up at it, and every one of them wants to be the King for All…!

##### iron-will › The Eastern Star (642)
[0] D(yushin): Well — is it enough now? / We have given Baekje a proper beating…
[1] D(yushin): So then… do you mean to drag the King of Baekje back too?
[2] D(chunchu): Brother… the grudge is mine. I know that. / But something else is moving, and it is not me moving it.
[3] D(chunchu): Brother… I had little interest in any of it. / A wife I loved, a peaceful household. / I believed that much would be enough. / But the world—
[4] D(yushin): Chunchu, what on earth are you saying…
[5] D(chunchu): The eastern star shines especially bright tonight… / Brother… let us go and take it now. / That old palace of ours… / the dream we had when we were young… / <b>The “King for All”, I mean…!</b>
[6] D(yushin): …I told you. That one is a planet.
[7] D(chunchu): Thirty years and you are still saying that.
[8] D(euija): Gyebek. You grew up inside that palace. / You have watched men go mad reaching for a chair. / <b>A man is one of two things — a king, or a slave.</b> / There are slaves in crowns and kings begging at the west gate. / One request.
[9] D(gyebek): I will obey.
[10] D(euija): No. Do not follow me. / One day I will give you a stupid order. More than one. / Judge it yourself. / I wear the crown. You are still the king of your own life…!
[11] D(gyebek): Your Majesty… why are you telling me this?
[12] D(euija): Gyebek… a man should hold a larger dream. / <b>The “King for All”, I mean…!</b>
[13] D(gyebek): Your Majesty. / I saw Gesomun again.
[14] p: He touches the left side of his neck when he says it, where the old burn scar runs down under his collar.
[15] p: The banquet hall has been scrubbed for three nights. Yeon climbs to a cave in the hill above the river. Nobody prays there lightly. The marches say the stone still remembers bowstrings.
[16] p: He kneels at the mouth and lays a crow-stamped ring-pommel on the stone. He does not ask forgiveness for the hall. He asks for witnesses.
[17] D(gesomun): The Holy King forged a country here. / I too… will forge one with my own hands.
[18] D(gesomun): …All my life I did not know what I was for. / Most men are born, and live a while, and die. / You gave me monsters. / <b>Thank you for giving me a direction.</b>
[19] D(gesomun): Until every bone in me is broken. / Until every jewel in my heart is cracked through. / I will not let go of this. / <b>The “King for All”, I mean…!</b>
[20] p: Gesomun wants a country. Far to the west, the man who owns half the world is trying to pronounce his name…!

##### epilogue › Emperor (643)
[0] p: Far to the west, a man who owns half the world hears a new name. He turns it over on his tongue, like a grape he hasn’t decided to eat.
[1] diagram: Tang court · 당 조정
[2] D(taizong): Gai Suwen…?
[3] p: The seventh invasion of Goguryeo has not begun. It has only found its excuse. Now it needs four dragons…!
